RagShortTexts: In 374 AD, Lazica governed from Archaeopolis (Nokalakevi), under the paramount rule of Kings of Lazica.
The polity asserted sovereign legitimacy anchored in Lazica dynastic heritage and royal assemblies.
Surrounded by shifting imperial and tribal pressures, the regime enforced loyalty through binding oaths and martial law.

Variants.Content: In 374 AD, the sovereign authority of Lazica anchored itself within Archaeopolis (Nokalakevi), confronting the accelerating tremors of Late Antiquity. Governed by Kings of Lazica, the state projected imperial legitimacy through dynastic lineage, military patronage, and strict codification of feudal oaths. Emphasizing institutional doctrine rooted in Lazica heritage, the crown mobilized loyal retinues and aristocratic councils to repel external encroachment. Beneath ceremonial grandeur lay unceasing vigilance against shifting steppe incursions and frontier uprisings, compelling the leadership to bind provincial magnates to the throne through land redistribution and martial alliance, safeguarding royal continuity amid an era of continent-wide transition.

Old sergeants of the royal guard sharpen blades beside a smoky fire. When the king's banners move out from the citadel, every man straps on iron armor and marches. Blood shed in the field is repaid with gold and land grants, and the old soldiers know a grant is worth only what the living heir chooses to honor. At the Lazica post, the night watchword is "Ridge."

A chancellor reads the royal decree aloud at the banquet, and the magnates raise their cups without a word. They will bow to it in public, but clan liberties and the tax revenue from their domains remain beyond the crown's reach. Each letter passing between the great houses repeats one condition: obedience holds only while the king guards noble privileges.
